quote: ist das Dreikörperproblem gelöst oder nicht?
english: Is the three-body problem solved or not?
topic: Hilbert contrasts proofs that use the Archimedean axiom, where the number of axiom applications can depend on the data, with non-Archimedean proofs that need a fixed number of steps, and then proposes finding a general method for stating problems precisely so that one can always decide whether they are solved.

triage.modern_statement: On the page this question is mainly an example of a broader point, not a separate research problem. Hilbert asks whether the classical Newtonian three-body problem counts as 'solved', and wants a precise standard for deciding when any problem is solved. In modern terms, the question is whether the general solution of three point masses under gravity can be given in a form that meets an agreed criterion. Possible criteria include closed form or enough algebraic or analytic first integrals (integrability), or a convergent series valid for all time. The broader proposal on the page, a general method for stating problems precisely so their status can always be decided, is the idea behind the decision problem (Entscheidungsproblem) that Hilbert later posed.
triage.answered_by: The answer depends on which criterion is used, and both were settled. (a) Integrability by first integrals: Bruns (1887) proved there are no further first integrals that are algebraic in positions and momenta beyond the classical ones. Painlevé and Poincaré extended this negative result. (b) Global series solution: Karl Sundman (1912) published a convergent power-series solution for all time, for the case where total angular momentum is not zero. Mathematicians including Poincaré had believed this kind of solution was impossible. Sundman's series converges far too slowly to be useful in practice, which shows exactly why Hilbert wanted a precise meaning of 'solved'. The general meta-question, a uniform method for deciding mathematical questions, was answered negatively by Church and Turing in 1936 through the Entscheidungsproblem.

evidence.claim: In 1912 the Finnish astronomer Karl Sundman published a solution to the three-body problem of a type that Poincaré and others had believed impossible.
Painlevé had conjectured that the three-body equations could be solved by power series once collisions are excluded. Sundman's 'complete solutions' later achieved this.
Bruns proved that there are no first integrals algebraic in positions and momenta other than the classical ones.
Painlevé generalized Bruns' theorem to integrals that are algebraic in the momenta and analytic in the coordinates.
Hilbert posed three questions at the 1928 international conference; the third became known as the Entscheidungsproblem. Church and Turing later showed it cannot be solved.

triage.why: The question is left open on the page and serves as an example of why 'solved' needs a precise definition. Under both standard modern readings it now has a definite answer: no further algebraic first integrals (Bruns 1887, extended by Painlevé and Poincaré), and a convergent global series exists (Sundman 1912). Whether a useless series really counts as 'solving' the problem remains a matter of definition, which was Hilbert's point. The three-body problem is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is still an active research area in celestial mechanics, for example periodic orbits and non-integrability, but I am basing that on general knowledge rather than a source cited here. I do not know the page's date, so I cannot say whether Hilbert wrote it before or after Sundman's work. That uncertainty, plus the example-like character of the question, is why confidence is medium.
